runs.prompt: A recipe for tomato soup: ingredients as a list, numbered steps, and a tip in a callout.

blocks.text: A simple, warming tomato soup that serves four and takes about 40 minutes.

items: 2 tbsp olive oil
1 tbsp butter
1 large onion, chopped
3 garlic cloves, minced
1 carrot, finely chopped
800 g canned whole tomatoes (2 cans)
500 ml vegetable stock
1 tsp sugar
1 bay leaf
Salt and black pepper to taste
100 ml cream (optional)
Fresh basil, to serve
Heat the olive oil and butter in a large pot over medium heat.
Add the onion and carrot and cook for 8–10 minutes until soft.
Stir in the garlic and cook for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the tomatoes with their juice, the stock, sugar and bay leaf.
Bring to a boil, then simmer gently for 20 minutes.
Remove the bay leaf and blend the soup until smooth.
Stir in the cream if using, and season with salt and pepper.
Serve hot, topped with torn basil.

blocks.text: Roast the tomatoes, onion and garlic at 200 °C for 30 minutes before simmering for a deeper, sweeter flavour.

blocks.text: How to Set Up a Home Herb Garden
Fresh herbs are easy to grow at home, whether on a windowsill, a balcony, or a small garden bed. Follow these six steps to get started.

items: Choose your location: pick a spot that gets at least six hours of direct sunlight a day, such as a south-facing window or a sunny patio.
Select your herbs: start with easy, versatile varieties like basil, parsley, chives, mint, thyme, and rosemary, and choose ones you actually cook with.
Pick containers with drainage: use pots at least 15 cm (6 in) deep with drainage holes, and give spreading herbs like mint their own pot.
Use quality potting mix: fill containers with a light, well-draining potting mix rather than garden soil, which compacts in pots.
Plant and water: set seedlings at the same depth they grew in their nursery pots, water thoroughly, then water again whenever the top 2–3 cm of soil feels dry.
Harvest and maintain: snip leaves regularly from the top to encourage bushy growth, pinch off flower buds, and feed lightly with a balanced fertilizer every four to six weeks.

blocks.text: With a sunny spot, good drainage, and regular harvesting, your herb garden will keep your kitchen stocked with fresh flavor all season long. Start small, learn what thrives in your space, and expand as your confidence grows.

runs.prompt: A decision record: context, the options considered as a list, the decision, and the consequences.

blocks.text: ADR-001: Adopt PostgreSQL as the primary datastore
Status: Accepted · Date: 2026-11-02 · Author: Ada Fjell

Our service currently stores data across several ad-hoc stores, which makes transactions, reporting and backups difficult. We need a single primary datastore that supports relational data, strong consistency, and mature operational tooling, while staying within the team's existing expertise.

items: PostgreSQL: relational, ACID transactions, rich ecosystem, team familiarity.
MySQL: relational and widely supported, but weaker support for some features we rely on (e.g. JSONB, partial indexes).
MongoDB: flexible schema, but multi-document transactions and reporting are harder for our relational data.
Keep the current mixed setup: no migration cost now, but ongoing complexity and consistency problems.

blocks.text: We will adopt PostgreSQL as the primary datastore for all new and migrated service data.

items: Positive: one consistent transactional store simplifies application code, reporting and backups.
Positive: the team can rely on existing PostgreSQL knowledge and tooling.
Negative: existing data must be migrated, which requires planning and a cutover window.
Negative: schema changes need migrations and review, reducing some flexibility.

runs.prompt: A troubleshooting guide for a printer that won't print: symptoms, three checks as numbered steps, and when to call support.

items: You send a job, but nothing comes out.
The job sits in the print queue as "Pending" or "Error".
The printer shows as "Offline" on your computer.
The printer's display or status light shows a warning.
Check power and connection: make sure the printer is on, and the USB cable or Wi-Fi/network connection is working. Restart the printer and your computer.
Check paper, ink and toner: load paper, clear any paper jam, close all covers, and replace empty ink or toner cartridges.
Check the print queue and settings: cancel stuck jobs, make sure the correct printer is set as default and is not paused or set to "Use Printer Offline", then print a test page.

blocks.text: Call support if the printer still won't print after all three checks, if it shows an error code that does not clear after a restart, if it makes grinding or unusual noises, or if you see any physical damage. Have the printer model, serial number and any error code ready.

runs.prompt: A short essay outline about why cities need more trees: introduction, three arguments as headings with one paragraph each, conclusion.

blocks.text: As cities grow denser and summers grow hotter, urban trees are often treated as decoration rather than infrastructure. This essay argues that trees are essential to healthy cities, offering measurable benefits for climate resilience, public health, and community life.
Trees Cool Cities and Reduce Heat Risk

Paved surfaces and buildings absorb heat, creating urban heat islands that can be several degrees warmer than surrounding areas. Tree canopies provide shade and cool the air through evapotranspiration, lowering street temperatures, reducing energy demand for air conditioning, and protecting vulnerable residents during heatwaves.

Trees filter airborne pollutants, capture fine particulate matter, and absorb carbon dioxide. Access to green streets is also linked to lower stress, better mental health, and more physical activity, making trees a low-cost contributor to the wellbeing of city dwellers.
Trees Strengthen Communities and Local Economies

Tree-lined streets invite walking, encourage people to linger, and make neighborhoods more attractive places to live and shop. Studies associate urban greenery with higher property values, stronger retail activity, and a greater sense of shared pride and safety in public spaces.

Trees cool our streets, clean our air, and bring communities together. Planting and maintaining more of them, especially in underserved neighborhoods, is one of the simplest and most effective investments a city can make in its future.

runs.prompt: A shell command cheat sheet: a heading, a bash code block with five common commands, and a paragraph for each group.

blocks.code:
ls -la                      # list all files with details
cd ~/projects               # change to a directory
grep -rn "TODO" src/        # search text recursively with line numbers
find . -name "*.log"        # find files by name
tar -czf backup.tar.gz dir/ # create a gzipped archive

blocks.text: Navigation: ls -la shows every file in the current directory, including hidden ones, with permissions, owner, size and modification time. cd moves you to another directory; cd on its own returns home and cd - jumps back to the previous one.

Searching: grep -rn walks a directory tree and prints each matching line with its file name and line number. find locates files by name, type, size or age; quote the pattern so the shell does not expand it first.
Archiving: tar -czf bundles a directory into a single gzip-compressed file. Swap c for x (tar -xzf backup.tar.gz) to extract it, or use t to list the contents without unpacking.

runs.prompt: A lesson summary on the water cycle with four stages as headings and a short paragraph under each.

blocks.text: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere. It is powered by energy from the Sun and by gravity, and it can be described in four main stages.

Heat from the Sun warms water in oceans, lakes and rivers, turning it from liquid into water vapour that rises into the air. Plants also release water vapour through their leaves, a process called transpiration.
As water vapour rises, it cools in the colder air higher up. The vapour condenses into tiny droplets of liquid water around specks of dust, and these droplets gather together to form clouds.
When the droplets in clouds join together and become too heavy to stay in the air, they fall back to Earth as precipitation. Depending on the temperature, this can be rain, snow, sleet or hail.

Water that falls to the ground collects in oceans, lakes and rivers, or soaks into the soil to become groundwater. Some flows over the land as runoff. From here, the Sun warms the water again and the cycle begins once more.

runs.prompt: A care guide for a fictional houseplant: light, water, soil and common problems, each as a heading with text.

blocks.text: The Silverleaf Moonfern (Lunafilix argentea) is a fictional houseplant with feathery, silver-veined fronds that seem to glow faintly at dusk. It is forgiving once settled, but it has firm opinions about light and water.

Give the Moonfern bright, indirect light, such as a spot a metre or two from an east- or north-facing window. Direct afternoon sun scorches the silver veins and turns them brown. In very low light the fronds stay green and lose their shimmer, so if the silver fades, move the plant somewhere brighter.

Keep the soil evenly moist but never soggy. Water when the top two centimetres feel dry, usually once a week in summer and every ten to fourteen days in winter. Use room-temperature water, since cold water can shock the roots. The Moonfern also enjoys humidity, so mist it or set it on a tray of damp pebbles.

Use a light, airy mix that drains freely: roughly two parts peat-free potting compost, one part orchid bark and one part perlite. Always use a pot with drainage holes. Repot every two years in spring, going up only one pot size at a time.

Brown, crispy frond tips usually mean the air is too dry or the plant has been underwatered. Yellowing, limp fronds with soggy soil point to overwatering or poor drainage, so let the soil dry out a little and check the roots for rot. Fronds that lose their silver sheen need more light. Watch for spider mites in dry conditions: wipe the fronds with a damp cloth and raise the humidity.

runs.prompt: A book review of a made-up novel: rating line, summary, what worked, what didn't, and a closing verdict.

blocks.text: Review: The Lantern Keeper of Vessa Bay
Rating: ★★★★☆ (4 out of 5) — Mireille Okonkwo-Hart, Harrow & Finch, 412 pages

In a fishing town on the edge of a northern sea, seventeen-year-old Ilse Marrow inherits the lighthouse her grandmother kept for fifty years, along with a ledger of every ship the lamp ever guided home. When she finds entries for vessels that never existed, and dates that have not yet happened, Ilse starts to suspect the light was doing more than warning sailors off the rocks. Okonkwo-Hart follows her through one winter as the town's secrets and the sea's patience both start to run out.

items: The setting is superb. Vessa Bay feels lived-in, from the salt-rotted piers to the gossip at the net-mender's shop.
Ilse is a sharp, stubborn narrator whose grief is handled with restraint rather than melodrama.
The ledger entries scattered between chapters are a clever device, rewarding readers who pay close attention.
The prose is quietly lyrical without tipping into purple.
The middle third sags. A subplot about a land developer adds little and stalls the momentum.
Several supporting characters, especially Ilse's cousin Tomas, are sketched too thinly to carry the emotional weight the ending asks of them.
The final reveal about the 'future ships' is explained a little too neatly, trading mystery for tidiness.

blocks.text: The Lantern Keeper of Vessa Bay is an atmospheric, moving debut that is easy to forgive for its uneven pacing. Read it on a stormy night with the lamp on. Recommended for fans of slow-burn literary mysteries with a touch of the uncanny.

runs.prompt: A Python snippet that reads a CSV file, in a code block, with a heading and a short explanation before and after.

blocks.text: Reading a CSV File in Python
Python's built-in csv module makes it easy to read tabular data. The snippet below opens a file and prints each row as a dictionary keyed by the column headers.

blocks.code:
import csv

with open("data.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    for row in reader:
        print(row)

blocks.text: DictReader uses the first line of the file as field names. Passing newline="" lets the csv module handle line endings correctly, and the with statement closes the file automatically when the loop finishes.

3. Traffic calming on Birch Lane. Several residents described cars cutting through Birch Lane at speed during the morning school run. Opinions differed between requesting speed bumps and asking for a seasonal 30 km/h limit. It was noted that the municipality prefers a written petition with signatures before considering either measure.

4. Winter lighting festival. The organising group proposed moving the festival from the square to the park to allow more stalls. Concerns were raised about accessibility of the park paths in icy conditions; the group will look into gritting and temporary lighting.

5. Community garden expansion. The garden committee reported a waiting list of eleven households for plots. A neighbouring strip of unused land owned by the housing cooperative could provide six additional plots if a lease can be agreed.
6. Any other business. A member asked that the notice board by the bus stop be repaired. Volunteers were requested for leaf clearing on 14 November.

items: The minutes of the June meeting were approved.
The treasurer's report was accepted.
A petition for a 30 km/h limit on Birch Lane will be drafted by Lars Eide and circulated by 15 November.
The winter lighting festival will be held in the park on 12 December, subject to a satisfactory safety plan.
The garden committee is authorised to negotiate a lease with the housing cooperative, with a budget of up to 3,000 NOK per year.
Tomas Berg will arrange repair of the notice board.

blocks.text: The meeting closed at 20:45. The next meeting will be held on Tuesday 26 January 2027.

Use a numbered list only when order matters; otherwise use bullets.
Keep items parallel: start each with the same part of speech.

runs.prompt: A short story opening of two paragraphs under a title, followed by a divider and an author's note.

blocks.text: The storm came in sideways that October, the way the old fishermen said only the worst ones did. Maren watched it from the lamp room, her palms flat against the cold glass, counting the seconds between the flashes of lightning and the answering growl that rolled across the water. Below her, the great lens turned on its bath of mercury, steady as a heartbeat, throwing its white arm out over the waves every twelve seconds. Her father had kept that rhythm for thirty-one years. Tonight, for the first time, it was hers alone to keep.

She did not see the boat until it was almost on the rocks. A small thing, low in the water, with no lantern and no sail, only a single figure hunched at the oars and pulling as if the sea itself were chasing it. Maren pressed closer to the glass. The beam swept past, and in that half-second of light the figure looked up, straight at the tower, straight at her, as though it had known all along exactly where she would be standing.

This opening grew out of a summer spent on the coast, where an abandoned lighthouse stood at the end of a long breakwater. I kept wondering who had last climbed its stairs, and what they had seen from the top. Maren is my answer, or the beginning of one.

runs.prompt: A checklist for publishing a blog post: draft, edit, images, links, schedule, with a tip callout.

blocks.text: Work through each step before you hit publish.

items.text: Draft: write the full post with a clear headline and structure
Edit: proofread for spelling, grammar, tone and length
Images: add a featured image, compress files and write alt text
Links: check every link works and points to the right page
Schedule: pick a publish date and time, then schedule the post

blocks.text: Read the post aloud once before scheduling. Awkward sentences are much easier to hear than to see.

runs.prompt: A summary of a fictional podcast episode: title, three key points, and a quote.

blocks.text: Episode 42: The Quiet Hours — Why Boredom Makes Us Creative

In this episode of the fictional podcast Slow Signals, host Mara Lindqvist talks with cognitive researcher Dr. Tobias Renn about what happens in our minds when we stop filling every spare moment with input.

items: Boredom is a signal, not a failure: it tells the brain to look for something more meaningful to do.
Constant phone checking cuts off the mind-wandering that links unrelated ideas together.
Short, scheduled 'empty' periods, such as a walk without headphones, gave Renn's study participants more original ideas.

blocks.text: The best ideas don't arrive when you're busy. They wait until you've run out of distractions.

runs.prompt: A personal values note: five values as headings, each with one sentence and an example, ending with a divider and a closing line.

blocks.text: I tell the truth even when it is uncomfortable. For example, I told my manager I had missed a deadline instead of making excuses.
I keep asking questions and learning new things. For example, I spend Sunday mornings reading about a topic I know nothing about.
I treat people with warmth and patience, especially when they are struggling. For example, I check in on a friend who has gone quiet rather than waiting for them to reach out.
I own my choices and follow through on my commitments. For example, when I promise to help a neighbour move, I show up on time.
I make room for rest, family and play alongside work. For example, I keep my phone off during dinner with my family.
These values are my compass; I return to them whenever I need to find my way.
